title: Perfect is His way
hook: perfect is His way and perfect His Word (Sukhmani 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pooraa, and your line: the perfect one. The salok rang it four times. Today: what does a perfect way look like on a day that isn't?

The car won't start. The rain comes in sideways. The email you were waiting for says no. By ten in the morning, the day is clearly not going to be a perfect one. Then Sukhmani's last ashtpadi says something that sounds almost cheeky on a day like that: perfect is His way, and perfect His Word. It isn't saying the car will start. It's saying something about what lies underneath the day that won't.
screen: `THE CAR WON'T START.` → `THE EMAIL SAYS NO.` → `PERFECT, UNDERNEATH?`

segments.voice: The twenty-fourth ashtpadi keeps ringing pooraa, perfect, through its stanzas. Its first stanza begins, in paraphrase: listen to the teaching of the perfect Guru; see the Supreme as near you; remember God with every breath, and the anxiety of the mind will lift. Perfect Guru, perfect Word, perfect way. Here's what perfect is not claiming. It isn't claiming every day will feel perfect, or that bad things don't happen. Sikh history has martyrdoms in it, Gurus among them. The tradition doesn't pretend life is smooth. What it claims is something underneath the surface: that God's hukam, God's order, is whole, even when we only see a ragged piece of it. Sikhs speak of meeting the day that way as bhaanaa mannanaa: accepting bhaanaa, God's will. Guru Arjan, who wrote Sukhmani, sings in another hymn, in paraphrase: whatever You do seems sweet to me. Sikh tradition remembers that he lived those words to the end. That's the trust this stanza points to. Not pretending the rain isn't sideways; trusting there's a whole beneath the part. And notice the practical line in the middle: remember God with every breath, and the anxiety lifts. Saas saas. The trust isn't one big leap. It's breath by breath, on the imperfect day itself. Perfect underneath, imperfect on top: Sukhmani asks the reciter to live in both.
screen: `THE PERFECT GURU, THE PERFECT WORD.` · `NOT A CLAIM THAT DAYS FEEL PERFECT.` · `BHAANAA: GOD'S WILL, ACCEPTED.` · `SAAS SAAS: BREATH BY BREATH.` · then, large: `PERFECT, UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Name to yourself, plainly, what's gone wrong today or this week, without arguing with it. Then, on each breath in, hold the thought, this is the surface, and on each breath out, there's a whole underneath; you don't have to feel the trust, just practice it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath.
Bhaanaa, God's will: Sukhmani says God's order and Word are whole even when our day isn't; Sikhs meet it with bhaanaa, breath by breath.
Your line: perfect, underneath. Breath by breath, even on the sideways-rain days. That's day five hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's last ashtpadi hear of the perfect Guru, Word and way, and meet hard days with bhaanaa, acceptance of God's will, remembering God with each breath.

chat.who: a friend having a rough week
chat.says: How can anyone call God's way perfect when everything's going wrong for me?
options: Sikhs speak of bhaanaa, God's will: a whole beneath the ragged part, trusted breath by breath.
It means nothing bad truly happens; hard days are only in your head, so just smile.
It means good days are perfect, and bad days come from somewhere else, not God.
chat.meaning: Sukhmani doesn't claim days feel perfect. It says God's hukam is whole beneath the ragged piece we see, and remembering, breath by breath, lifts the anxiety.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): bhaanaa means God's will; acceptance is bhaanaa mannanaa, so the gloss is corrected. Removed the uncited count ('two Gurus') under the claims rule, the sweeping 'nobody in this tradition', and a line telling the listener what they feel.
Paraphrase of ashtpadi 24 pauri 1 (poore gur kaa sun updes; paarbrahm nikat kar pekh; saas saas simrahu gobind; man antar kee utrai chind): confirm.
The outline's 'perfect is His way and perfect His Word' is treated as the ashtpadi's theme; a Keeper may point to a specific line.
Asa M5 (teraa keeaa meethaa laagai) at Ang 394: confirm. Guru Arjan's martyrdom in 1606 is referenced without detail.
